blogs.title: When Expert Testimony Crumbles: The Federal Circuit Reinforces Limits on Contradictory Infringement Opinions
blogs.description: This post examines the Federal Circuit's analysis of Dr. Wells' expert testimony and how the court determined that contradictory and confusing testimony cannot sustain a jury verdict. The decision cites Johns Hopkins University v. Datascope Corp. and illustrates the boundary between permissible expert disagreement and testimony so inconsistent that no reasonable jury could rely on it. The post will discuss the practical implications for litigators in preparing expert witnesses and the standards for JMOL when expert testimony pivots mid-cross-examination without clear explanation.

blogs.title: Prosecution History Estoppel or Mere Amendment? The Court Draws a Line on 'Clear and Unambiguous' Disavowal
blogs.description: This post analyzes the Federal Circuit's treatment of Finesse's amendment from 'two or three signals' to 'three signals' during prosecution of the '775 patent. The court applied the Continental Circuits standard and found the amendment did not constitute a 'clear and unambiguous' disavowal of two-signal implementations. The post will explore the distinction between claim amendments made to overcome prior art and those that rise to the level of prosecution history disclaimer, and how this decision fits into the broader doctrine of prosecution history estoppel in patent law.

blogs.title: Claim Limitations as Technical Impossibilities: When the Accused Product Literally Cannot Infringe
blogs.description: This post focuses on the '134 patent's claim limitation requiring sampling of 'signals of interest' and 'interference generating signals' together, and how the expert's own testimony revealed a fundamental timing problem—the interference generating signals are created downstream after sampling occurs. The post will examine how claim drafting creates technical requirements that can categorically preclude infringement, regardless of expert attempts to map claim language onto accused products, and the importance of understanding signal flow when litigating method claims.
